children.text: jayati sa dainyagadākulam akhilam idaṃ paśyato jagad yasya
children.translated_text: Victorious is he, whose compassion, seeing this whole world afflicted with the disease of wretchedness,
melted within his very heart and became embodied as <s>rasa</s> (mercurial essence).
Then, wearing yellow garments, conqueror of <s>Bali</s>, whose mount is <s>Garuḍa</s> rich in passion for the destruction of serpents,
victorious is that one born of <s>Hara</s>, like <s>Hari</s>, who has split apart the burden of the misery and wretchedness of existence.

children.text: mūrchitvā harati rujaṃ bandhanamanubhūya muktido bhavati
children.translated_text: After being swooned, it removes disease; after undergoing bondage, it becomes a giver of liberation.
When well-killed it makes one immortal. Who else is a mine of compassion apart from <s>sūta</s> (mercury)?
Even that incurable disease, born from the mass of sins consisting in violence against gods, teachers, cows, and twice-born men,

children.text: tadapi ca śamayati yasmāt ko 'nyas tasmāt pavitrataraḥ ||
children.translated_text: it pacifies; therefore who else is purer than that?

children.text: tasya svayaṃ hi sphurati prādurbhāvaḥ sa śāṃkaraḥ ko 'pi
children.translated_text: Indeed its manifestation shines forth of itself, somehow belonging to <s>Śaṃkara</s>.
For how otherwise could it pacify sinful disease merely by appearing?

children.text: rasabandhaśca sa dhanyaḥ prārambhe yasya satatamiva karuṇā
children.translated_text: Blessed is that binding of <s>rasa</s> at whose beginning there is always, as it were, compassion:
'When <s>rasa</s> is perfected, I shall make the earth free from old age and death.'
And those who, without abandoning the body, have obtained a body born from the creation of <s>Hara</s> and <s>Gaurī</s>,
those accomplished adepts of <s>rasa</s> are worthy of reverence, for hosts of mantras are their servants.

children.text: sukṛtaphalaṃ tāvadidaṃ sukule yajjanma dhīśca tatrāpi
children.translated_text: This much is the fruit of merit: birth in a good family, and intelligence even there;

children.text: sāpi ca sakalamahītalatulanaphalā bhūtalaṃ ca suvidheyam ||
children.translated_text: and that intelligence too has as its fruit the mastery of the whole surface of the earth, and the earth is easily brought under control.
The fruit of control over the earth is wealth, and wealth has various enjoyments as its fruit.

children.text: bhogāḥ santi śarīre tadanityamaho vṛthā sakalam ||
children.translated_text: Enjoyments exist in the body; but that body is impermanent. Ah, all of it is vain.
Thus, having understood wealth, body, and enjoyments to be always impermanent, one should strive

children.text: muktau sā ca jñānāt taccābhyāsāt sa ca sthire dehe ||
children.translated_text: for liberation; and that comes from knowledge, that from practice, and that from a stable body.

children.text: tatsthairyaṃ na samarthaṃ rasāyanaṃ kimapi mūlalohādi
children.translated_text: No <s>rasāyana</s> (elixir), whether root, metal, or the like, is capable of giving that stability,

children.text: svayamasthirasvabhāvaṃ dāhyaṃ kledyaṃ ca śoṣyaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: being itself unstable by nature, burnable, wettable, and dryable.

children.text: kāṣṭhauṣadhyo nāge nāgaṃ vaṅge vaṅgamapi līyate śulve
children.translated_text: Wood and herbs dissolve in lead; lead dissolves in tin; tin too dissolves in copper;

children.text: śulvaṃ tāre tāraṃ kanake kanakaṃ ca līyate sūte ||
children.translated_text: copper dissolves in silver, silver in gold, and gold dissolves in <s>sūta</s> (mercury).
As all beings certainly dissolve into the supreme self,
so that one king of <s>rasa</s> makes the body free from old age and death.

children.text: amṛtatvaṃ hi bhajante haramūrtau yogino yathā līnāḥ
children.translated_text: Just as yogins absorbed in the form of <s>Hara</s> attain immortality,
so gold, iron, and the rest, when the ether has been swallowed up, are absorbed in the king of <s>rasa</s>.
A man whose body is stable, through the force of practice, obtains knowledge endowed with the eight qualities
and reaches the state of <s>Brahman</s>, no longer afflicted by the suffering of dwelling in rebirth.

children.text: ekāṃśena jaganti ca viṣṭabhyāvasthitaṃ paraṃ jyotiḥ
children.translated_text: The supreme light stands supporting the worlds with one part;
that immortal reality, with its three parts, is not easily attained by mere dispassion.
For with a body that is in every way distressed by disease, old age, death, and pain,
momentary and fragile, one cannot worship that subtle <s>Brahman</s>.
Who would even utter the name of yogic accomplishment without the body,
when the stainless reality, attainable through yoga, is not within the range even of the mind?
From sacrifice, giving, austerity, Vedic study, self-restraint, and good conduct,
the highest good is, they say, self-realization through the power of yoga.
Conscious bliss, from which abundant conceptual distinctions have melted away and which is devoid of all objects,
even if it has shone forth, what can it do for the class of beings whose body has not shone forth?
The conscious light, situated between the two eyebrows, pure like fire and lightning and illuminating the world,
opens for certain makers of merit.
It should be known as consisting solely of supreme bliss, supreme, of the nature of light, free from conceptual division,
with all afflictions gone, peaceful, and self-experienced.
Placing the mind in that, seeing the whole world shining forth,
one whose bonds of karma have been destroyed attains <s>Brahman</s>-hood here itself.
Sense-objects indeed set, because of the conjunction of breath and the inner organ;
there is no shining of the darkness of the senses, and therefore no pleasure or pain from what shines forth.
Men free from passion and hatred, truthful in conduct and devoid of falsehood,
become without distinctions everywhere through contact with consciousness-<s>Brahman</s>.
Endowed with <s>aṇimā</s> and the other powers, with radiant bodies, joyful and always blissful, they remain,
having attained the immortal state of <s>Brahman</s> and being truly fulfilled.
The one abode of the sciences, the root of <s>dharma</s>, wealth, desire, and liberation:
what higher good is there than the body made free from old age and death?
He who does not know <s>sūtaka</s> (mercury) even by the valid means of direct perception
how will he know the conscious god whose form is unseen?
That which is shattered by old age and has fallen under the sway of suffering such as cough and breathlessness
is not fit for <s>samādhi</s>, for the range of its intellect and senses is obstructed.
As a child of sixteen, a mortal is intent on tasting the flavors of sense-objects; afterwards,
when discernment has arisen, he is old. How could he attain liberation?

children.text: asminn eva śarīre yeṣāṃ paramātmano na saṃvedaḥ
children.translated_text: For those who in this very body have no awareness of the supreme self,
after abandoning the body that <s>Brahman</s> is still farther away.

children.text: brahmādayo yajante yasmin divyāṃ tanuṃ samāśritya
children.translated_text: In whom <s>Brahmā</s> and the others worship, taking refuge in a divine body,
and other living-liberated sages endure until the end of the aeon.
Therefore, by a yogin who desires liberation while living, first of all
a divine body must be made through union with the creation of <s>Hara</s> and <s>Gaurī</s>.
And in the method of accomplishing that, a wise person must first carefully understand
the eighteen <s>saṃskāras</s> (purificatory operations), made pure by the preparatory operation.
Heating, rubbing, swooning, reviving, distilling, restraining, and regulating...
And then there are the measure for kindling, swallowing <s>gagana</s> (mica), and the procedure of <s>cāraṇa</s> (feeding).
Likewise there are liquefaction in the womb, external liquefaction, digestion, coloring of mercury, and transmission of its essence,
penetration, piercing, and ingestion: thus the operations of mercury are eighteenfold.
With equal parts of āsurī, salt, the three pungents, citraka, fresh ginger, and radish,
mercury should be steamed with sour gruel for three days over a gentle fire.
With jaggery, burnt wool, salts, soot from a house, brick-powder, and āsurī,
each measured as a sixteenth part of the mercury, it should be ground with sour gruel for three days.
Impurity, fire, and poison are said to be the three natural defects of mercury.

children.text: mūrchāṃ malena kurute śikhinā dāhaṃ viṣeṇa mṛtyuṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Through impurity it causes stupefaction, through fire burning, and through poison death.

children.text: gṛhakanyā harati malaṃ triphalāgniṃ citrakaśca viṣam
children.translated_text: Gṛhakanyā removes the impurity, triphalā the fire, and citraka the poison.
Therefore one should repeatedly stupefy it seven times with these substances mixed together.
By this rubbing, mercury becomes thoroughly purified and freed from lead and tin.
It rises in the distillation apparatus from the sour-gruel decoction.
After making a paste with copper, it is distilled because of suspicion of lead and tin.

children.text: tasmindoṣān muktvā nipatati śuddhas tathā sūtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having abandoned its defects there, the mercury descends purified in the same way.
The lower vessel should be eight fingers broad and ten fingers long,
raised four fingers below the neck, with a water-reservoir made in it.
Above it should be placed a flattened pot whose lower vessel-mouth enters within, with the rim of its own mouth immersed in water,
and whose belly is sixteen fingers wide.
When mercury, freed from all defects, is made to descend into that upper vessel,

children.text: sutarāṃ bhavati rasendro dravye ca rasāyane yogyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the lord of mercury becomes especially fit for substances and for rasāyana preparations.
Having made a vanished paste with triphalā, fire, śigru, mustard, and salts,
one should smear it on the upper vessel and cause it to descend downward with blazing one-pala fires.
Or, placed in a lamp-apparatus and freed from all defects,
the king mercury should be distilled by the method of transverse distillation.
A finely powdered sheet of mica, joined with mercury and with sour gruel,

children.text: khalve dattvā mṛditaṃ yāvat tannaṣṭapiṣṭatām eti ||
children.translated_text: should be placed in a mortar and ground until it reaches the state of a vanished paste.
One should use mercury that has been distilled by transverse distillation, and, successively, over a strong fire,
after steaming it, distil it; as long as the fire is strong it does not fall.
Afflicted by grinding, stupefaction, and distillations, because of weak potency it becomes impaired.
But when its replenishment is obtained by restraint with the waters of creation-lotuses, it will not be impotent.

children.text: iti labdhavīryaḥ samyak capalo'sau saṃniyamyate tadanu
children.translated_text: Thus, having properly obtained potency, that mobile mercury is then restrained,
through steaming with phaṇinayana, ambuja, arka, vajra, karkoṭī, and ciñcikā.
With bhūkhaga, borax, and pepper, and with salt, āsurī, śigru, and sour gruel for three days,
that mercury, kindled by steaming, becomes desirous of a morsel.
When the king mercury, thus kindled and purified, shines like a thousand flashing streaks of lightning,

children.text: bhavati yadā rasarājaś cāryo satvādi tadā bījam ||
children.translated_text: then the seed beginning with sattva should be fed to it.

children.text: pītakriyāsu pītaṃ śvetaṃ tārakriyāsu mukham ādau
children.translated_text: For yellow operations, yellow material; for white silver-operations, first the mouth should be white.

children.text: deyaṃ khalve ghṛṣṭo divyauṣadhibhiḥ sa nirmukhaś carati ||
children.translated_text: Ground in a mortar with divine herbs, it moves even without a mouth.

Thus ends the second instruction, consisting of the purification of mercury, in the <s>Rasahṛdayatantra</s> composed by the venerable <s>Govindabhagavatpāda</s>, teacher among supreme-haṃsa renunciants.
Those who, without compact seed-feeding, think themselves accomplished merely by gaining leaves and the like,
are wretches who, having reached the ocean, are satisfied with obtaining a cowrie shell.
But others, being great, disregarded wealth, elephants, kingship, the Kaustubha jewel, and the like,
and obtained the supreme nectar; becoming immortal, they became gods.
By steaming with alkaline herbs, salts, and acids there is awakening of hunger and fixation of color,

children.text: na punaḥ pakṣacchedo dravatvaṃ vā vinā gaganam ||
children.translated_text: but there is no cutting of the wings nor liquidity without <s>gagana</s> (mica).

children.text: abhrakajīrṇo balavān bhavati rasastasya cāraṇe proktāḥ
children.translated_text: Mercury that has digested mica becomes powerful; for its feeding are taught
the great procedures involving binding, impregnation, herbs, without-mouth and with-mouth states.

children.text: niścandrikaṃ hi gaganaṃ kṣārāmlairbhāvitaṃ tathā rudhiraiḥ
children.translated_text: Mica without moonlike glitter, treated with alkalis and acids and also with blood,
ground with drops of the three waters of creation and with tumburu juice, is consumed by mercury.
Mica enclosed in a heating packet with water of yava and ciñcikā, mixed with its root, śatāvarī, and gadā,
and treated with the juices of ghanarava, śigru, and punarnavā, is consumed by mercury.
Āranāla, mixed with sarjī, kṣitikhaga, borax, and salt, and kept for three days in a vessel of arka,
is praised for treating mica and related substances.
In that liquid one should melt purified lead and quench it a hundred times,

children.text: vaṅgaṃ vā tāravidhau rasāyane naiva tadyojyam ||
children.translated_text: or tin for a silver operation; it should not be used in a rasāyana preparation.
Powders of mica, mercury, auxiliary minerals, nectar, metals, and rasāyana substances,
indeed everything whatever that is a substance for feeding, should be treated with this.

children.text: ādau khalve mṛditāṃ piṣṭīṃ hemnaśca tāṃ rasaścarati
children.translated_text: At first, mercury consumes in the mortar that ground paste of gold;

children.text: tārasya tārakarmaṇi dattvā sūte tato gaganam ||
children.translated_text: for a silver operation, after placing silver in the mercury, then mica is added.
When mica, gold, iron, and the like are placed bit by bit in a mortar and ground in the essence,
the lord of mercury consumes them with kṣitikhaga, vetasa, and citron acids.

children.text: samukhaṃ nirmukhamathavā tulyaṃ dviguṇaṃ caturguṇaṃ vāpi
children.translated_text: It may be with-mouth or without-mouth, equal in quantity, double, quadruple,
eightfold, sixteenfold, or even multiplied thirty-two times.

children.text: iti pattrābhrakam uktaṃ tena vidhānena cārayetsūtam
children.translated_text: Thus leaf-mica has been described; by that method one should feed mercury.
The morsel, the paste, and the womb: feeding has these three marks.
Those by whom mica, processed in various ways by the swing-method,
has been prescribed in the procedure of feeding have not seen it being blown away.
Other people too, of worthless understanding, think that the powder of copper paste ground down with sulfur,
when shaken up by the swing-procedure, is mercury that has digested it.
When the mercury has been heated with oil and the like, by means of a pellet-mouth of gold, silver, and similar metals,

children.text: carati ghanaṃ rasarājo hemādibhir eti piṇḍatvam ||
children.translated_text: the compact <s>rasarāja</s> (king mercury) moves and, with gold and the rest, reaches the condition of a lump.

children.text: anye svacchaṃ kṛtvā śukapicchamukhena cārayanti ghanam
children.translated_text: Others, after making it clear, feed the compact substance through a parrot-feather mouth,
by the method taught by adepts, with a morsel already eaten, not with a dry one.
Or else pyrite and mica, in equal parts, mixed with salt and cooked,
when thrown into an iron vessel, at the end of steaming consume black mica.
I shall teach that instruction by which sulfur and mica are introduced,

children.text: pakṣachinnaś ca raso yogyaḥ syād rasarasāyanayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: whereby mercury, with its wings cut, becomes fit for mercury-work and for rasāyana.
Sulfur is said to impart color to the king mercury, to be capable of cooking and digesting the seeds,
to cut the wings of <s>sūtaka</s> (mercury), and to be useful in binding mercury.

children.text: dattvā khalve truṭiśo gandhakam ādau rasaṃ ca truṭiśo'pi
children.translated_text: Having first put sulfur bit by bit in a mortar, and mercury also bit by bit,
one should grind them until that paste is formed.

children.text: tadanu ca drutabalivasayā samabhāganiyojitaṃ tathā gaganam
children.translated_text: After that, mica should likewise be combined in equal quantity with melted Bali fat,

children.text: truṭiśo rasaṃ ca dattvā kurvīta yathepsitāṃ piṣṭim ||
children.translated_text: and, adding mercury bit by bit, one should make the desired paste.
That too is then dropped downward in the lamp-apparatus with blazing cow-dung cakes.
Afterwards the mercury, freed from impurity, has its wings cut by the mica and sulfur.

children.text: bhasmākāraś ca raso hemnā saha yujyate sa ca dvaṃdve
children.translated_text: Mercury in ash-like form is joined with gold, and that is used in the pairing.

children.text: athavā gandhakapiṣṭiṃ paktvā drutagandhakasya madhye tu ||
children.translated_text: Or, after cooking sulfur-paste, in the midst of melted sulfur,
that gold-paste too is further cooked in sulfur.

children.text: itthaṃ hemnā sūto milati dvaṃdve tathā kṣaṇānmriyate ||
children.translated_text: In this way mercury unites with gold in the pairing, and thus is killed in an instant.

children.text: itare pakṣacchedaṃ dvaṃdve rasamāraṇaṃ na vāñchanti
children.translated_text: Others do not desire the cutting of the wings and the killing of mercury in the pairing.

children.text: bījānāmapi pākaṃ hṛṣyanti ca tadanu tapyanti ||
children.translated_text: They rejoice even in the cooking of the seeds, but afterwards they suffer.
Knowing the feeding of mica to involve so many faults and much labor in this way,
a procedure is set forth that accords both with practical operation and with śāstra.
The living principle is ungraspable, unstained, subtle in movement, pervasive, and imperishable.

children.text: yāvadviśati na yonau tāvadbandhaṃ kuto bhajate ||
children.translated_text: So long as it does not enter a womb, how can it undergo bondage?

Thus ends the third instruction in the tantra called <s>Rasahṛdaya</s>, composed by the venerable <s>Govindabhagavatpāda</s>, teacher among supreme-haṃsa renunciants, consisting of the feeding of leaf-mica with a mouth, included within the impregnation with a mouth after the impregnation without a mouth.

children.text: kṛṣṇo raktaḥ pīto yo 'bhraḥ syāt sthūlatārakārahitaḥ
children.translated_text: Mica that is black, red, or yellow, free from coarse stars,

children.text: vajrī sa pītakarmaṇi pātitasattvo ghano yojyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and diamond-like, with its sattva cast down, should be used in yellow operations.

children.text: niścandrikaṃ hi gaganaṃ vāsitamapi vāsanābhir iha śatadhā
children.translated_text: For even if mica without moonlike glitter has here been treated a hundred times with impregnations,

children.text: tadapi na carati rasendraḥ sattvaṃ kathamatra yatnataḥ prabhavet ||
children.translated_text: mercury still does not consume it; how could its sattva be produced here with effort?
Apart from mica-sattva alone, nothing else is capable of cutting off the wings.

children.text: tena niruddhaprasaro niyamyate badhyate ca sukham ||
children.translated_text: By it mercury, whose range has been checked, is easily controlled and bound.
The person who tries to bind mercury without cutting its wings

children.text: bījaireva hi sa jaḍo vāñchatyajitendriyo mokṣam ||
children.translated_text: is a dull man who, with the seeds alone and with his senses unconquered, desires liberation.

children.text: nādhaḥ patati na cordhvaṃ tiṣṭhati yantre bhaved anudgārī
children.translated_text: It neither falls downward nor rises upward; it remains in the apparatus and does not belch forth.
Mercury that has digested mica should be known as having its wings cut.
The four colors beginning with white have been described; these are free from coarse stars.

children.text: vajrī satvaṃ muñcatyapare dhmātāśca kācatāṃ yānti ||
children.translated_text: The diamond-like variety releases sattva; the others, when blown, turn to glass.
Whatever compact micas are mentioned in the world as white, red, black, and yellow,
they are weak and without sattva; the diamond-like one is the best of all.

children.text: sūte'pi rasāyanināṃ yojyaṃ parikīrtitaṃ paraṃ satvam
children.translated_text: For mercury too, the supreme sattva proclaimed for practitioners of rasāyana should be employed.

children.text: trividhaṃ gaganamabhakṣyaṃ kācaṃ kiṭṭaṃ ca pattrarajaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There are three inedible forms of mica: glass, slag, and leaf-powder.

children.text: muñcati satvaṃ dhmātas tṛṇasāravikārakair ghanaḥ svinnaḥ
children.translated_text: Compact mica, steamed with substances made from straw-essence, releases sattva when blown.
After rejecting the glass and slag, one should carefully take the essence.
After steaming and binding it into a lump with buffalo curds, milk, urine, dung, and ghee,
then, when joined with the five cow-products, it causes sattva resembling iron to fall.
Metals that have drunk mercury in the heat of the sun release only a little sattva.

children.text: svasthānasthāḥ santo muñcanti ta eva bhūyiṣṭham ||
children.translated_text: But those same metals, remaining in their own place and intact, release very much.
When strongly and deeply blown, the cloud rains with streams of gold.
One should recognize the fallen sattva as spotless, like the mouth of a god.

children.text: yadi lohanibhaṃ patitaṃ jātaṃ gaganasya tadrasaścarati
children.translated_text: If what has fallen is like iron, then that product of mica is consumed by mercury.

children.text: milati ca sarvadvandve hyauṣadhibhiścarati vināpi mukhaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And it unites in every pairing; by means of herbs it moves even without mouths.

children.text: mākṣikasahitaṃ gaganaṃ dhmātaṃ satvaṃ mukhapradaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: Mica together with pyrite, when blown, becomes a sattva that grants a mouth.

children.text: tadanu ca nāgairvaṅgaiḥ sahitaṃ ca mukhapradaṃ satvam ||
children.translated_text: After that, sattva together with lead and tin also grants a mouth.
Through combination with pyrite-sattva, <s>sūtaka</s> (mercury) consumes the whole of mica-sattva.

children.text: niyataṃ garbhadrāvī sa rajyate badhyate caivam ||
children.translated_text: Certainly it melts substances in the womb; in this way it is colored and bound.

children.text: satvaṃ ghanasya kāntaṃ tālakayuktaṃ surundhitaṃ dhmātam
children.translated_text: The attractive sattva of mica, joined with <s>tālaka</s> and well confined, is blown.
Here, after three repetitions, the sattva becomes supremely effective for binding <s>rasendra</s> (mercury).
Iron and mica-sattva, made to flow with an equal part of <s>tālaka</s>, are consumed.
And by the abhiṣava operation, when rubbed with the finger, that melts in the womb.
Then tin and mica-sattva, made to flow with six parts of <s>tālaka</s>, are consumed.
And by the abhiṣava operation mercury moves and proceeds; there is no doubt about this.

children.text: bahalaṃ suvarṇavarṇaṃ niculapuṭaiḥ patati pañcabhiḥ satvam
children.translated_text: A dense sattva, golden in color, falls through five nicula-heatings;
it is made into pellets, a dead <s>gagana</s> (mica), stainless and free from slag.
Having powdered that, then the dense substance, repeatedly impregnated with alkalis and acids,
and ground with drops of the three creation-waters and with tumburu juice, moves into action.
Dense sattva, copper, and pyrites, combined in equal portions and thoroughly mixed,

children.text: tacchulbābhraṃ kathitaṃ carati raso jīryati kṣipram ||
children.translated_text: that is called copper-mica; mercury consumes it, and it is quickly digested.
Thus dense sattva, together with tāpya and copper, ground in an iron mortar,
is consumed by the lord of mercury with the acids of sour gruel, vetasa, citron, and bījapūra.

children.text: iti tīkṣṇaśulbanāgaṃ mākṣikayuktaṃ ca tatkṛtaṃ khoṭam
children.translated_text: Thus the khoṭa made from sharp iron, copper, lead, and joined with pyrites,

children.text: tadbhasma ca puṭavidhinā nirvyūḍhaṃ satvarañjakaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: and its ash, extracted by the heating-packet method, becomes a quick colorant for sattva.

children.text: cāryaṃ yatnena rase ghanasatvaṃ tadvidhaṃ ghanaṃ tasya
children.translated_text: That kind of dense sattva should be carefully fed to mercury; its dense substance,
having been combined with all the seeds, should be carried through by mixing the pairs.
First comes the feeding of mica; at the end comes the feeding of the womb-melt of gold.

children.text: yo jānāti na vādī vṛthaiva so'rthakṣayaṃ kurute ||
children.translated_text: One who does not know this is no true disputant; he merely wastes his wealth in vain.
I shall state one secret of swallowing <s>gagana</s> (mica), from the combination of dense substance and arka:
with effort it consumes only mica-sattva, not the whole body.

children.text: yadi ghanasatvaṃ garbhe na patati no vā dravanti bījāni
children.translated_text: If the dense sattva does not fall into the womb, or if the seeds do not melt,
and if there is no conjunction with external melting, how can mercury be bound here?
A morsel lacking womb-melting, even when digested, does not attain unity.

children.text: ekībhāvena vinā na jīryate tena sā kāryā ||
children.translated_text: Without becoming one it is not digested; therefore that must be done.

children.text: bījānāṃ saṃskāraḥ kartavyaḥ ko'pi tādṛśaḥ prathamam
children.translated_text: First, some such processing of the seeds must be performed,
by which they melt in the womb of the king mercury through the class of acids.
Gold into which an equal quantity of pyrites has been cast, and which is joined with an equal quantity of pyrites-sattva,

children.text: garbhe dravati ca jarati ca jaritaṃ badhnāti nānyathā sūtam ||
children.translated_text: melts in the womb and is digested; when digested, it binds mercury, and not otherwise.
Pyrites-sattva, melted in mercury and digested with gold beginning from a quarter part,
produces an ariṣṭa of silver and excellent gold by coating on leaves.
If the morsel has reached homogeneousness, has passed through cloth, and is greater in weight on the scale,

children.text: grāso drutaḥ sa garbhe drutvāsau jīryate kṣipram ||
children.translated_text: then that molten morsel, after melting in the womb, is quickly digested.

children.text: na biḍairnāpi kṣārairna snehairdravati hemaṃ tāraṃ vā
children.translated_text: Gold or silver does not melt by salts, nor by alkalis, nor by oils,
without pyrites-sattva that has been kept for three days with red coloring matter.
Salt soaked in the juice of devī, and snake-leaf powdered on a stone:
after three heatings this, well killed, should be placed in an iron vessel.
A broad, large cup should be made half a finger deep, with its mouth serving as the support;
over it another cup should be placed, raised by one finger.
It should have three holes made in it; in the holes four fingers higher,
iron rods are to be fitted, and on them also the gold leaves.
Having been set in place, they are fumigated; fire should be kindled beneath the apparatus.
Merely from being coated by the smoke, the gold leaves become black.
Those leaves, heated by fire and then killed in the apparatus by smoke,
by the procedure for cooked gold, are consumed by the lord of mercury and melt in the womb.
By that very method, a silver leaf should be steamed by the apparatus procedure;

children.text: jāyeta kṛṣṇavarṇaṃ tattāraṃ dravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: that silver becomes black in color and melts in the womb.
Or, with powerful tin, by the apparatus procedure called lead,

children.text: hemāhvaṃ tāraṃ vā dravati ca garbhe na sandehaḥ ||
children.translated_text: what is called gold, or silver, melts in the womb; there is no doubt.
Rasaka joined with the powerful substance, by the procedure previously stated,

children.text: pakvaṃ cūrṇaṃ yāvadbhavati bhṛśaṃ dravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: is cooked until it becomes a powder; it melts intensely in the womb.
Then gandhaka-stone, extracted a hundred times, likewise in excellent gold

children.text: sūte ca bhavati piṣṭirdravati hi garbhe na vismayaḥ kāryaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and in mercury becomes a paste; indeed it melts in the womb, and no wonder should be felt.
Or excellent rasaka, extracted a hundred times in purified gold, is an excellent seed.

children.text: bījaṃ jarati rasendre dravati ca garbhe na sandehaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The seed is digested in the lord of mercury and melts in the womb; there is no doubt.

children.text: athavā tālakasatvaṃ śilayā vā tacca hemni nirvyūḍham
children.translated_text: Or tālaka-sattva, or that with śilā, extracted in gold,

children.text: śataguṇamatha mūṣāyāṃ jarati rasendro dravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: then a hundredfold in a crucible, is digested by the lord of mercury and melts in the womb.
Mercury, cinnabar, mica, tāpya, vimala, nectar, copper, iron, and parpaṭikā,
lead ground with the milks of snuhī and arka and joined with kaṃkuṣṭha and śilā,
that, together with mica, tālaka, conch, and mercury, heated again and again,
and mixed with tamarind alkali, causes tin to become lifeless.

children.text: vidhinānena ca puṭitaṃ mriyate nāgaṃ nirutthatāṃ ca gatam
children.translated_text: Heated by this method, lead is killed and brought to non-revival;

children.text: vaṅgaṃ ca sarvakarmasu niyujyate tadapi gatajīvam ||
children.translated_text: tin too, lifeless, is employed in all operations.

children.text: mṛtanāgaṃ mṛtavaṅgaṃ mṛtavaraśulvaṃ mṛtaṃ tathā tīkṣṇam
children.translated_text: Dead lead, dead tin, dead excellent copper, and likewise dead sharp iron,

children.text: ekaikaṃ hemavare śatanirvyūḍhaṃ dravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: each one extracted a hundred times in excellent gold, melts in the womb.

children.text: samagarbhe drutikaraṇaṃ hemno vakṣyāmyahaṃ paraṃ yogam
children.translated_text: I shall state a further supreme method for making the melting of gold in an equal womb:
powder of bhrāmaka and sasyaka, extracted a hundred times, is the great seed.
Or, having applied the smoke of sulfur, the smoke of tālaka, and that of śilā-named rasaka,
one should set a very long downward-facing crucible in half of a potsherd.

children.text: ūrdhvaṃ lagnā piṣṭī sudṛḍhā ca yathā tathā ca kartavyā
children.translated_text: The paste adhering above should be made firm and solid, in whatever way is necessary.
Having placed it on the back of the potsherd, one should then burn daityendra.

children.text: stokaṃ stokaṃ dattvā karṣāgnau dhmāpayenmṛdā liptām
children.translated_text: Adding it little by little, one should blow it with a karṣa-fire, smeared with clay.

children.text: garbhe dravati hi bījaṃ mriyate tathādhike dāhe ||
children.translated_text: For the seed melts in the womb, but it is killed when the burning is excessive.
Sulfur, tālaka, śailā, sauvīraka, rasaka, gairika, and darada,
together with alkalis, acids, and salts, form the viḍa, with equal parts of mākṣika, vaikrānta, and vimala.
Having made a gold paste, well ground and well wrapped with this very mixture,

children.text: tripuṭaistapte khalve mṛditā garbhe tathā dravati ||
children.translated_text: when it is heated with three puṭas and ground in a hot mortar, it melts in the womb.

children.text: rakte śatanirvyūḍhaṃ netrahitaṃ bhasma vaikrāntakaṃ cātha
children.translated_text: Next, red vaikrāntaka ash, extracted a hundred times and useful for the eyes,

children.text: vimalaṃ śatanirvyūḍhaṃ grasati samaṃ dravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: and vimala extracted a hundred times, consumes an equal amount and melts in the womb.
Whatever viḍa-compounds there are, and alkalis, acids, salts, and the fiery group,
all of them, when extracted a hundred times, are declared to produce womb-melting.
When extracted a hundred times the amount is equal; when extracted seventy-five times, it is a quarter less.
At fifty times it is half of that; at twenty-five times it should be a quarter.
At half of that it is an eighth; at half of that extraction it is a sixteenth.
At half of that it is one thirty-second, and at half of that extraction it is one sixty-fourth.
Thus this womb-melting has been explained, by the method of impregnation and by the class of acids.

children.text: svedanavidhinā jñātvā mṛditāṃ tapte tu khalvatale ||
children.translated_text: Knowing it by the steaming procedure, it should be ground on the surface of a hot mortar.
Having understood the strength and weakness of the seed, the grinding procedure performed on the king mercury,

children.text: svedavidhānaṃ ca puṭaṃ yantraṃ vā vihitarasakarma ||
children.translated_text: the steaming method, the puṭa, the apparatus, and the prescribed mercury operation,

children.text: sūtavaraṃ lakṣayate bījaṃ nopekṣatāṃ yathā yāti
children.translated_text: one observes the excellent mercury, so that the seed does not go to a state of neglect.
In that way the operation should be performed by the rule, the good procedure taught at the feet of the guru.

children.text: bāhyadrutirati vimalā sphurati hi keṣāṃcideva siddhānām
children.translated_text: External melting, exceedingly pure, appears only for certain perfected adepts.

children.text: tebhyaḥ samyak jñātvā kalanāḥ kāryāstathā drutayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having learned the calculations properly from them, the meltings should then be carried out.

children.text: varanāgaṃ rasarājaṃ bījavaraṃ sāritaṃ tathā tritayam
children.translated_text: Excellent lead, the king mercury, the excellent seed, and likewise the threefold sārita,
together with sulfur and śilā, becomes free from lead when treated with a lamp-wick.

children.text: baddhvā sudṛḍhe vastre poṭalikāyāṃ śikhīkṛto dīpaḥ
children.translated_text: Having tied it in a very firm cloth as a bundle, the lamp is made into a flame,

children.text: taile magnaṃ kṛtvā nirnāgaṃ jāyate kṣipram ||
children.translated_text: and, when immersed in oil, it quickly becomes free from lead.

children.text: kṛtvātra dīrghamūṣāṃ sudṛḍhāṃ dhmātaṃ tu bhasmagartāyām
children.translated_text: Here one should make a long, very firm crucible and blow it in a pit of ashes.
Having put in śilā-powder, then mercury, and then śilā-powder again,
one should cover it with ash and blow it until it cools by itself.

children.text: ākṛṣya tatra sūtaṃ jñātvā nāgaṃ subhakṣitaṃ sakalam ||
children.translated_text: Drawing out the mercury there, one should know that all the lead has been well consumed.

children.text: jñātvā nāgaṃ truṭitaṃ punarapi dadyādyathā bhavettriguṇam
children.translated_text: Knowing that the lead has been broken down, one should add it again until it becomes threefold.
Afterwards, having purified it, one should then combine it with the excellent seed.

children.text: athavā tāraṃ vaṅgaṃ sūtaṃ saṃsārya vaṅgaparihīnam
children.translated_text: Or, having processed silver, tin, and mercury, with the tin removed,
by the tālaka procedure, likewise by the apparatus procedure it becomes free from tin.
Or it is tied in cloth, combined with girijatu, well wrapped with māṣa beans,

children.text: pakvaṃ taile vaṭakaṃ nirvaṅgaṃ jāyate nūnam ||
children.translated_text: and cooked in oil as a cake; it certainly becomes free from tin.
Having made a paste-column, it is then processed with the excellent seed,

children.text: athavā baddharasena tu sahitaṃ bījaṃ surañjitaṃ kṛtvā ||
children.translated_text: or, together with bound mercury, the seed is made well colored.

children.text: gandhakanihitaṃ sūtaṃ nihitānihitaṃ ca śṛṅkhalāyāṃ tat
children.translated_text: Mercury placed in sulfur, and that placed and not placed in a chain,
when joined with extracted mercury, certainly produces womb-melting.

children.text: sūtakabhasmavareṇa tu bījaṃ kṛtvā rasendrake garbhe
children.translated_text: With excellent ash of mercury, after making the seed in the womb of the lord of mercury,

children.text: mṛditā piṣṭī vidhinā hyabhiṣavayogāddravati garbhe ca ||
children.translated_text: the paste, ground by the rule, melts in the womb through the method of impregnation.

children.text: patrābhrakaṃ ca satvaṃ kāṃkṣī vā kāntamākṣikaṃ puṭitam
children.translated_text: Leaf-mica and its sattva, or kāṅkṣī, kānta, or mākṣika, heated in puṭas,
with nirguṇḍī, gṛhakanyā, cāṅgerī, and palāśa greens,
should be heated in puṭas until it has the appearance of vermilion essence.
With salt remaining to one quarter, it is cooked firmly by the pot-cooking method.
Each one, extracted a hundred times, should digest the excellent seed for the lord of mercury.

children.text: garbhe dravati ca kṣipraṃ hyabhiṣavayogena mṛditamaṅgulyā ||
children.translated_text: It quickly melts in the womb when ground with the finger by the method of impregnation.
Even after melting, it should be melted again; lead should be cast into excellent shining gold.
With a triple addition of śilā, that is taught as serpent-seed.

children.text: vaṅgaṃ tu tena vidhinā hemavare kṣepya tālavāpena
children.translated_text: Tin, by that method, is cast into excellent gold with an addition of tāla.
Or, in silver, the excellent seed is extracted through combination with the broken-down material.

children.text: yo niḥsṛto bhujaṅgād rasakeśarīvajrapañjaraḥ sa punaḥ
children.translated_text: That which has issued from the serpent, again like a mercury-lion in an adamantine cage,
crooked by the quality of serpent-gold, is renowned by the name rasāṅkuśa.

children.text: evaṃ pakvaṃ vidhinā bījavaraṃ sūtarāṭ tathāmlena
children.translated_text: Thus the excellent seed, cooked by the rule, should be treated by the king mercury with acid,
and should be well steamed until the paste becomes smooth.

children.text: tailena tena vidhinā svinnā piṣṭī bhavedakhilam
children.translated_text: By that same method, when steamed with oil, the whole becomes a paste.
Or the seed rubbed smooth on a stone becomes a lump.
Cooking should be done by the cake-method, with the use of oil.
Having placed it in a penetrating lump, and with māṣa beans, it becomes a very firm lump.
It is well cooked with a gentle fire until the lump is not burnt.

children.text: ākṛṣya cātha sūtaṃ piṇḍe śeṣaṃ tathā punaḥ pācyam ||
children.translated_text: Then, having drawn out the mercury, the residue in the lump should again be cooked in the same way.
Or, in a medicinal lump, on a potsherd heated in a swing-apparatus, according to the rule,
it should again be placed in the lump, in the womb, until melting occurs.

children.text: evaṃ drutaṃ hi garbhe bījavaraṃ jarati rasarāje
children.translated_text: Thus, melted in the womb, the excellent seed is digested in the king mercury.
Without womb-melting, it is digested in the womb by means of viḍa-compounds.
Having thus caused the morsel to be consumed, then the womb-melting is placed on birch bark,
smeared with salt, alkali, acid, lime, fragrant urine,
bound externally with firm cloth, and the morsel should be digested by swing-steaming.
It is done in a pot half-filled with sauvīra, or else with alkaline urines.
By this procedure, one should digest the morsel in periods of three days each.
Now, after taking it up from the apparatus, the sign of what is digested should be known.
As soon as it has been taken up, it should then be washed in a vessel with sour gruel.
And because the sour gruel is contaminated, it should then be removed by the use of cloth.

children.text: tadanu sukhoṣṇe pātre saṃmardyo'sau yathā na hīye
children.translated_text: After that, in a pleasantly warm vessel, it should be rubbed so that it is not diminished,
until all the sour gruel adhering to it dries up.
Thus, with its water dried away and made quite pure by hand-rubbing,
it should be squeezed over a vessel with a cloth folded four times.

children.text: yadi parigalitaḥ sakalo vastrād grāsena caikatāṃ yātaḥ
children.translated_text: If all of it has filtered through the cloth and has become one with the morsel,

children.text: na bhavati yadi daṇḍadharo jīrṇagrāsastadā jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and if it does not become rod-bearing, then the morsel should be known as digested.
Having taken the undigested paste away from the morsel and mercury, one should place it in the apparatus.

children.text: svastho bhavati rasendro grāsaḥ pakvaḥ punarjarati ||
children.translated_text: The lord of mercury becomes sound; the morsel, once cooked, again undergoes digestion.
In the swing-apparatus four morsels are to be digested in proper sequence,
and the remaining ones in the tortoise-apparatus, until it digests twice as much or more.
At the beginning, here, no fixed rule about the measure of the morsel can be made,

children.text: grasate na hi sarvāṅgaṃ gaganamato lakṣaṇairjñeyam ||
children.translated_text: for it does not consume the whole mica in every case; therefore it is to be known by its signs.

children.text: yadi hi catuḥṣaṣṭyaṃśān grasati rasastadā dhareddaṇḍam
children.translated_text: If mercury consumes one sixty-fourth part, then it holds a rod;
on entering one fortieth part it has the form of milk-rice.
At one thirtieth part it takes the form of a leech, and at one twentieth it is free from spluttering;
from one sixteenth it is like something cut; beyond that the morsel is hard to digest.
After first digesting mica-sattva with these five morsels,
one skilled in womb-melting digests the seed by sixteenth parts.
Smoky, making a crackling sound, moving like a frog, and trembling too,
then becoming motionless, mercury should be understood to have digested mica.

children.text: kapilo'tha nirudgārī vipluṣabhāvaṃ ca muñcate sūtaḥ
children.translated_text: Then mercury becomes tawny, belchless, and gives up the state of spluttering;
motionless and without movement, it should be understood to have digested mica.
In the middle of a vessel filled with water, a very broad potsherd should be placed,
and on top of it, in the center, mercury should be set; after that, against the wall,
it is to be covered with a light iron bowl, sealed at the cloth-and-clay joint,
and that whole potsherd should be filled with embers mixed with dung and chaff.
Through steaming and rubbing, mercury placed in the tortoise-apparatus digests;
then, by the very strength of fire, there is womb-melting of all metals.

children.text: evaṃ dattvā jīryati na kṣayati raso yathā tathā kāryaḥ
children.translated_text: Having given it in this way, mercury should be treated so that it digests and does not diminish.
With alkalis and viḍas it wastes away, but with auxiliary rasas it vomits up the morsel.

children.text: grāsaṃ na muñcati na vāñchati taṃ ca bhūyaḥ kāṃścidguṇānbhajati bhuktavibhuktimātrāt
children.translated_text: It does not release the morsel, nor does it desire it again, and it acquires certain qualities merely from having eaten and separated from it.

children.text: yajjīryate pracurakevalavahniyogāt tasmādviḍaiḥ suniviḍaiḥ saha jāraṇā syāt ||
children.translated_text: Since what is digested is digested through the application of abundant fire alone, therefore digestion should be done together with very compact viḍas.
With viḍas made from sauvarcala salt, the three pungents, kāṅkṣī, kāsīsa, and sulfur,
śigru, and substances impregnated a hundred times with mercury, it digests even copper leaves.
Ash of wholly burnt mūlaka root, filtered with the urine of a fragrant animal,
and impregnated a hundred times with the fat of a sacrificial victim: by that, gold is digested instantly.
Plantain, palāśa, sesame, nicula, kanaka, suradālī, vāstukā, and castor,
together with varṣābhū, vṛṣa, and mokṣaka, are alkali plants, according to availability.

children.text: ānīya kṣāravṛkṣān kusumaphalaśiphātvakpravālairupetān kṛtvātaḥ khaṇḍaśastān vipulataraśilāpiṣṭagātrātiśuṣkān
children.translated_text: Having brought alkali trees furnished with flowers, fruits, roots, bark, and sprouts, then cutting them into pieces and drying their bodies well after grinding them on a very broad stone,

children.text: dagdhvā kāṇḍaistilānāṃ karisurabhihayāmbhobhir āsrāvya vastrair bhasma tyaktvā jalaṃ tanmṛduśikhini pacedvaṃśapākena bhūyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: one should burn them with sesame stalks, leach them through cloths with the waters of elephant, cow, and horse, discard the ash, and cook that water again over a gentle flame by the bamboo-cooking method.

children.text: tacchuṣyamāṇaṃ hi sabāṣpabudbudān yadā vidhatte kṣaṇabhaṅgurān bahūn
children.translated_text: When, as it dries, it produces many vaporous bubbles that burst in a moment,
then one should add the three pungents, asafoetida, sulfur, the three alkalis, the six salts, and bhūkhaga.

children.text: dravyāṇi saṃmiśrya nivṛtya bhūtale vyavasthitaṃ śastrakaṭorikāpuṭe
children.translated_text: Having mixed the substances, removed it, and set it on the ground in an iron bowl-pellet,
one should place it for seven days among grain; it is then to be used for mercury digestion and the like.
Through combination with the acids of jambīra, bījapūraka, cāṅgerī, and vetasa,
alkalis become especially excellent for womb-melting and digestion.
At first, having given the viḍa in lower and higher order, in the amount of one eighth of the mercury,
one should perform digestion in this way, gradually increasing the fire step by step.
The lord of mercury that has digested mica displays a luster corresponding to the mica-sattva:

children.text: kṛṣṇāṃ raktāṃ pītāṃ sitāṃ tathā saṃkarairmiśrām ||
children.translated_text: black, red, yellow, white, and also mixed by combinations.
With black mica the lord of mercury is strongly joined with dark colors;

children.text: śvetai raktaiḥ pītairvahneḥ khalu varṇato jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: with white, red, and yellow varieties, it is indeed to be known by the color of the fire.

children.text: atha nijakarme varṇaṃ na jahāti yadā sa rajyate rāgaiḥ
children.translated_text: Now, when in its own operation it does not abandon its color and is dyed by colors,
then, gradually cleansed by the processes to be explained, it performs coloring.
Strength resides in mica-sattva; digestion-colors are established in sharp iron;
binding is in sāra iron, while sāra-producing is from lead and tin.

children.text: krāmati tīkṣṇena rasastīkṣṇena ca jīryate kṣaṇādgrāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Mercury moves with sharp iron, and with sharp iron the morsel is digested in a moment;
sharp iron is the womb of gold, and by sharp iron it takes on colors.

children.text: tadapi ca daradena hataṃ kṛtvā mākṣikeṇa ravisahitam
children.translated_text: And even that, killed by cinnabar and prepared with pyrites together with copper,

children.text: vāsitamapi vāsanayā ghanavaccāryaṃ ca jāryaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: even when perfumed by perfuming, is to be made to consume and to be digested like mica.

children.text: kāntaṃ vā tīkṣṇaṃ vā kāñcīṃ vā vajrasasyakādīnām
children.translated_text: Magnetite, or sharp iron, or kāñcī, or one among vajrasasyaka and the others,
or all of them together: in the coloring of mercury, a mixture is desired.

children.text: kuṭile balamabhyadhikaṃ rāgastīkṣṇe tu pannage snehaḥ
children.translated_text: In the crooked metal the power is greater; in the sharp serpent-metal there is indeed oiliness for coloring.
But in the lotus-metal, the knowers of metals declare color, oiliness, and strength.
With all these metals, killed by pyrites and likewise melted in the womb,
the king mercury, digested by the conjunction of viḍa, attains color.
With tālaka, darada, and śilā, together with oil, alkali, acid, and salt,
one should carry out a heating, in equal, double, and triple quantities, for tin, weapon-metal, and the others.
By sprinklings with red oily substances one should complete what remains; this is the drawing-out of mercury.
Merely through cāraṇa and jāraṇa it makes the mercury like the indragopa insect.

children.text: athavā kevalam amalaṃ kamalaṃ daradena vāpitaṃ kurute
children.translated_text: Or else pure lotus-metal alone, cast with darada, makes
mercury three times consumed and digested, resembling lac juice.
Of tāpya, sulfur, and śilā, treated with the liquefied animal water of the red group,
even one, when cast into dead lotus-metal, colors the king mercury.
External coloring by sulfur occurs when the color has been disturbed; in manaḥśilā and tāla,
only pyrites-sattva and rasaka are praised for coloring.
When gold and rasaka are made to proceed in sequence, purified, and blown in a mute crucible,

children.text: triguṇaṃ cīrṇo jīrṇo hemābho jāyate sūtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: mercury, three times consumed and digested, becomes golden in appearance.

children.text: atha kṛṣṇābhrakacūrṇaṃ puṭitaṃ raktaṃ bhavettathā sakalam
children.translated_text: Then black mica powder, heated in a sealed furnace, should likewise become wholly red.
Mercury, three times consumed and digested, becomes like molten gold.

children.text: triguṇena mākṣikeṇa tu kanakaṃ ca mṛtaṃ rasakatālayutam
children.translated_text: Gold that is dead with threefold pyrites, joined with rasaka and tāla,
and cooked together with salt in a pot until it resembles the indragopa insect,

children.text: taccūrṇaṃ sūtavare triguṇaṃ cīrṇaṃ hi jīrṇaṃ tu
children.translated_text: that powder, threefold, when consumed in the best mercury and then digested,
makes the mercury like molten gold, and it colors all metals.
Sattva is eight times the leaf; molten metal is eight times the sattva;
seed is eight times the molten metal; therefore one should digest the seed.

children.text: iti rakto'pi rasendro bījena vinā na karmakṛdbhavati
children.translated_text: Thus even when the lord of mercury is red, without seed it does not become effective in operations.
That seed is of two kinds, yellow and white; this is applied only when perfected.
Its purification is manifold, by powders of mica, mercury, subsidiary minerals, and metals.

children.text: dvividhaṃ bījaṃ tairapi nāśuddhaiḥ śudhyate vai tat ||
children.translated_text: Even with these, the twofold seed is not purified if they themselves are impure.
But if someone performs the operation with these while they are impure, his mercury becomes

children.text: avyāpakaḥ pataṃgī na rase rasāyane yogyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: non-pervasive and merely colored like an insect; it is not fit for mercury alchemy.
Vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, adri, darada, and rasaka
are the eight rasas; likewise their sattvas are rasāyanas.
Sulfur, gairika, śilā, lakṣitīkhecara, añjana, and kaṃkuṣṭha:
this is known as the group of subsidiary minerals; śikhi and śaśin are called sāra-metals.
Copper, ara, sharp iron, kānta, mica-sattva metals, tin, and lead
are said to be called pūti; their purification must be performed.
Sauvarcala, saindhava, kacūlikā, sāmudra, romaka, and biḍa:
these are the six salts; and there are svarjī, ṭaṅkaṇa, and yavakṣāra alkalis.

children.text: sūryāvartaḥ kadalī vandhyā kośātakī ca suradālī
children.translated_text: Sūryāvarta, kadalī, vandhyā, kośātakī, suradālī,
śigru, vajrakanda, nīrakaṇā, and kākamācī:
with the juice of any one of these, when repeatedly treated with salt, alkali, and acid,
the rasas and subsidiary minerals are purified; when blown, they release their sattvas.
Vaikrānta, steamed with alkalis and acids and then blown, forcibly melts.
That becomes purified merely by melting; kānta is purified by treatment with hare's blood.
Sasyaka too, well treated with substances of the red group and sprinkled with oily coloring matter,

children.text: śudhyati vāraiḥ saptabhirataḥ paraṃ yujyate kārye ||
children.translated_text: is purified in seven turns; after that it is employed in the operation.
Vimala, treated first with alkalis and oils and afterward with acid,

children.text: śudhyati tathā ca rasakaṃ daradaṃ mākṣikamapyevam ||
children.translated_text: is purified; and rasaka, darada, and mākṣika are purified in the same way.
Even a thin leaf smeared with salt, alkali, acid, the milks of arka and snuhī,

children.text: dhmātaṃ nirguṇḍīrasasaṃsiktaṃ bahuśo bhaveddhi raktaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: and blown, when repeatedly sprinkled with the juice of nirguṇḍī, indeed becomes red.

children.text: śudhyati nāgo vaṃgo ghoṣo raviṇā ca vāramapi munibhiḥ
children.translated_text: Lead and tin are purified, and also ghoṣa, by copper, even once, according to the sages,
with sprinklings of nirguṇḍī juice and with castings of the powder of its root.
Sharp iron, treated and heated with the liquefied animal water of the red group, is indeed colored.
It is purified when treated with the juice of the kadalī and śikhi and heated three times.

children.text: sarvaṃ śudhyati loho rajyati suragopasannibho vāpāt
children.translated_text: Every metal is purified and is colored, from casting, like the red suragopa insect,

children.text: mākṣikadaradena bhṛśaṃ śulvaṃ vā gandhakena mṛtam ||
children.translated_text: by pyrites and darada intensely; or copper is killed by sulfur.
Now the emergence of sattva will be described.
Vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, and the others, without sattva,

children.text: śuddhā api no dvandve milanti na ca tān raso grasati ||
children.translated_text: even when purified, do not combine in a compound, nor does mercury consume them.
The substance called nāganāsikā, moon-water, nectar, having acquired hardness,
binds rasa-vaikrānta in this way, and binds mercury by its own sattva.
That stone of many different shapes, born on the peaks of the mountain of the immortals,
is best in flowing water; after obtaining that mountain-water stone,
it should be forcibly blown with two bellows, firmly bound with the five māhiṣas.
One should add one-tenth parts of svarjikā, salt, ṭaṅkaṇa, and guñjikā alkalis.
It goes to hardness and releases sattva in the form of sparks.
That, like a heap of pearls, should be taken, while the glassy portion is rejected.
Rasa-vaikrānta thus combines, joined in a compound, equally with gold.
When the compact sattva has been drawn out, mercury thereby attains binding.
Of all the metals and minerals, beginning with vajra, mica, kānta, sasyaka, and mākṣika,
this solid lump, blown with firm charcoal, causes their <s>sattva</s> (essential metallic extract) to fall out.
Apart from the sattva of mākṣika, the others have no power to kill metal;

children.text: na patati tāvatsatvaṃ bhastrānte na yāvad āhriyet ||
children.translated_text: the sattva does not fall until it is drawn out at the end of the bellows operation.

children.text: raktaṃ mṛdu nāgasamaṃ satvaṃ yasmāddhi mākṣikātpatitam
children.translated_text: Since the sattva fallen from mākṣika is red, soft, and like lead,
that of sulfur-stone also should likewise be carefully made soft.
Mākṣika, well roasted with salt and acid and ritually ground with acid,

children.text: muñcati soṣṇe grāsam āyasapātre tu piṣṭikā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: releases its morsel when hot; in an iron vessel it becomes a paste.

children.text: tutthāddhi tāpyajasamaṃ samasṛṣṭaṃ patati vai satvam
children.translated_text: From tuttha, when mixed equally with tāpya, sattva indeed falls in the same way;
in the case of mica, vaikrānta, kānta, and the like, it resembles iron.
Tāpya, treated a hundred times with the milk of strīvajrī and with castor oil and then blown,

children.text: evaṃ tribhiriha vāraiḥ śulvasamaṃ bhavati rañjakaṃ haimam ||
children.translated_text: in this way, here after three turns, becomes like copper, a golden coloring agent.
Tāpya, treated a hundred times with plantain juice and thoroughly cooked with honey and castor oil,

children.text: tāpyaṃ muñcati satvaṃ rasakaṃ caivaṃ trisantāpaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: releases sattva, and rasaka does so too by three heatings in this way.
A lump made from wool, ṭaṅkaṇa, jaggery, pura, lac, sarjarasa, and all metals ground together

children.text: chāgīkṣīreṇa kṛtā piṇḍī śastā hi satvavidhau ||
children.translated_text: with goat's milk is excellent in the procedure for sattva.
Having carefully taken thirty palas of the powdered sattva ingredients,
together with seven palas of ṭaṅkaṇa and joined also with three palas of guñjā,
and having mixed them with sesame powder, iron-slag palas, and fish in double proportion,
one makes a wheat-bound lump, repeatedly treated with the five products of the cow.
By the furnace-blowing method, with the fierce fire of bellows, that falls;
and mica-sattva melts, and likewise all the sattvas.
Now the carrying-through of the <s>bīja</s> (seed) is begun.

children.text: svīkṛtya sarvasarito gaṅgā jaladhau yathā tathā haimam
children.translated_text: Just as the ocean, taking all rivers into itself, is the Gaṅgā, so gold,
after entering mercury and taking in the qualities of all metals, unites with it.

children.text: jīryati milati ca śulbe tatsatvaṃ kiṭṭatāṃ yāti
children.translated_text: It is digested and combines with copper; its sattva turns into slag.
In operations with gold it is carried through with karin and tin, and in operations with silver likewise.

children.text: ghanasatvaṃ khalu raviṇā rasāyane dvaṃdvakaṃ yojyam
children.translated_text: Compact sattva should indeed be joined with copper in rasāyana as a compound pair,
with mountain-born substances, mākṣika, ochre, and darada treated by the falling of the red group.
One should make a remaining seed from soft copper, kānta, compact sattva, killed lead, sharp iron, and gold,
or by casting with darada, śilā, tāla, and mākṣika.

children.text: mṛtanāgaṃ vaṅgaṃ vā śulvaṃ ghanasatvatārakanakaṃ vā
children.translated_text: Killed lead, or tin, copper, compact sattva, silver, or gold,
when blown, all becomes just that, through mountain-born substances or through stronger purifications and castings.

children.text: raktagaṇaṃ pītaṃ vā mākṣikarājāvartam atho vimalam
children.translated_text: The red group, or the yellow group, or mākṣika, rājāvarta, or vimala,
or any one of them, together with ochre, kunaṭī, kṣitigandhaka, and khaga, may be used.
Only by substances carried through does mercury take on color and the like and attain binding;
carried through with killed metals, subsidiary minerals, and the like, it becomes chain-seed.
Carried through by iron rods, and by what are called non-compounds and mixtures,
with mercury and metals, it becomes suitable for the operation of digestion.
This seed, sprinkled in the red group and cast with it,
colors and binds mercury as soon as it has been made to move and digest.
For all seeds, with killed metals, mercury, and the like purified by red unctuous substances,

children.text: bījānāṃ kuru vāpaṃ raktasnehe niṣekaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: one should perform casting, and sprinkling in red unctuous matter.
Tin-mica, mica-silver, the two white tins struck by white mountain-ore,
and the red struck by white tāpya color the carried-through tin-mica.
This procedure of carrying-through has been revealed for the pacification of all defects;
for seeds too, in this way, compact sattva is first joined.
Having made from goat-bone ash a crucible in the shape of a small bowl,
with dense pores at the joining of leaves and smeared with ṭaṅkaṇa, poison, and guñjā,
now the joining of compounds will be explained.

children.text: yāvan nāṅgāṅgatayā na milanti lohāni sarvasattveṣu
children.translated_text: So long as metals do not combine as limb and body in all sattvas,

children.text: tāvatsarvāṅgaṃ na ca carati raso dvandvayogena ||
children.translated_text: so long mercury does not move through every limb by the joining of compounds.
Metal cast with any one of mākṣika, rasaka, sasyaka, or darada,
when well blown, abandons its dense condition and unites with sattva.
In rasāyana, a compound should be used with jaggery, pura, ṭaṅkaṇa, lac, and sarjarasa,

children.text: strīstanyena tu piṣṭaiḥ rasāyane dvaṃdvitaṃ yojyam ||
children.translated_text: combined with dhātakī and ground with woman's breast milk.
With wool, ṭaṅkaṇa, mountain-born substance, earwax, eye-dirt, indragopa, and crabs,

children.text: nārīpayasā piṣṭaiḥ sarve dvandveṣu hi milanti ||
children.translated_text: ground with a woman's milk, all metals indeed unite in compounds.
Thus mercury and vaikrānta combine, joined as a compound, equally with gold;
when that sattva has been carried through, mercury thereby attains binding.
For every compound, seed is excellent with mountain-born substance, lelītaka, indragopa, and the like,
with buffalo earwax and similar substances, with ṭaṅkaṇa, salt, and poisons.
With these also, when mixed with honey, silver-mica combines, as do tāpya and gold;
and with castor oil, ṭaṅkaṇa, kaṃkuṣṭha, śilā, and indragopa.
Having thoroughly ground purified gold with mercury and made it joined with equal mica,
one should prepare, as a quarter part, any one of the compounds previously stated.
Having added purified mākṣika, twice as much as the mercury, subsidiary mineral, and gold,
one should grind it with the fresh juice of kākamācī and with plantain bulb.
When this lump has been made, gold-mica combines in a diamond crucible;
in this way the sattvas beginning with mica combine with copper, silver, and sharp iron.
The procedure for composite seeds and the like is by union with <s>gagana-sattva</s> (mica essence).
Something other than the pyrites combination may be used, but everywhere it must necessarily be joined.
For all the sattvas, <s>kānta-mukha</s> is the first agent of combination.
Together with the paste previously described are pyrites, killed lead, orpiment, and realgar.
Thus ends the twelfth instruction, consisting of the section on pairs, in the <s>Rasahṛdayatantra</s> composed by the venerable <s>Govindabhagavatpāda</s>, teacher of paramahaṃsa renunciants.
Pyrites with <s>kānta</s> and sharp iron; sharp iron with pyrites and mica: these are a seed.
Pyrites, <s>kānta</s>, and copper; sharp iron and mica: these are a great seed.
Pyrites, <s>kānta</s>, and copper, and also copper, mica, and pyrites;
<s>kānta</s>, mica, and pyrites; tāpya, copper, and mica: these are a great seed.
Pyrites, sharp iron, and copper; sharp iron, copper, and mica: these are a great seed.
Pyrites, <s>kānta</s>, and gold; gold, copper, and pyrites: these are a great seed.
Pyrites, sharp iron, and silver; and likewise silver, copper, and pyrites;
also <s>kānta</s> with copper and tāpya, and copper, mica, tāpya, and gold;
<s>kānta</s>, moon-metal, grain-metal, and tāpya; and <s>kānta</s>, mica, sharp iron, and pyrites;
gold, mica, copper, and tāpya; or gold, mica, copper, and pyrites;
<s>kānta</s>, mica, copper, and tāpya: the composite seeds are sixty-four.
At the beginning of all seed preparations, after making the combination as stated,

children.text: śatavāpyaṃ yadvahnau drāvitaṃ hi bījaṃ viśuddhamidaṃ ||
children.translated_text: the seed which has been melted in fire should be roasted a hundred times; this is the purified seed.

children.text: na patati yadi ghanasatvaṃ garbhe no vā dravanti bījāni
children.translated_text: If compact sattva does not fall into the womb, or if the seeds do not melt,
and if there is no conjunction with external liquefaction, how can mercury be bound here?

children.text: samād adhi ca yajjīrṇaṃ bījaṃ tenaiva cāvartatā kāryā
children.translated_text: With that seed which has been digested for more than a year, the turning operation itself should be performed.
That procedure must be done, because from it gold indeed arises.
After melting it in an iron vessel, one should add mercury with a quarter-part of sulfur.
Then, grinding it with the juice of herbs, one should make a pill.

children.text: saṃsthāpya lohaphalake chāyāśuṣkāṃ tu tāṃ vaṭikām
children.translated_text: Having placed that pill on an iron plate and dried it in the shade,
one should cover it with a small iron bowl and coat it very firmly.
Smeared with salt-moistened clay, it should be made very firm in order to block the smoke.
After placing strong coals on it, it should be heated smokelessly with the fire of two bellows.
It should be blown until the pellet becomes red in appearance.
Then, after removing the coals and judging that the bowl has cooled naturally,
one should dig out and dig out again; then the rasa is to be taken from the bowl.

children.text: eṣaḥ mṛtasūtarājo golakavadbhavati ca sa sukhādhmātaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This king of killed mercury becomes like a ball, and it is easily blown.
When intensely blown with glass and borax, it becomes a single rasa like a peacock's throat.
One should add tin threefold, then lead in sequence, in very small portions.
Afterward the mercury-seed, which effects the binding of mercury, should be joined with gold.
Also with orpiment-mercury, making a pill with restraining herbs,

children.text: evaṃ nigṛhya dhūmaṃ sudhiyā rasamāraṇaṃ kāryam
children.translated_text: the wise person should thus restrain the smoke and perform the killing of mercury.

children.text: athavā śilayā sūto mākṣikayogena vā siddhaḥ
children.translated_text: Or else, mercury perfected by realgar, or by union with pyrites,
becomes white in color through smoke-blocking, or through those two.
With powder of killed copper and tāpya, joined with <s>kānta</s>, one should color the pellet.
When brought out and joined with compact sattva and gold, it is to be used in rasāyana.

children.text: balinā triguṇena rasāt parpaṭikayutena marditaṃ sūtam
children.translated_text: Mercury ground with powerful material three times the quantity of the mercury and mixed with parpaṭikā,
is made into a pill with restraining divine herbs and dried in the shade.
Having enclosed it in the middle of parpaṭikā set in a crucible, with a concealed and very firm covering,
when blown, it becomes a pellet joined with gold, effecting the binding of mercury.
Parpaṭikā mixed with powerful material is ground, treated with snuhī and arka, and made into a pill.
A hollow should be made in the middle; then it is filled with mercury and covered.

children.text: bāhye dattvā nigaḍaṃ suliptamūṣodare dṛḍhaṃ nyastam
children.translated_text: Having put a clamp on the outside and placed it firmly inside a well-coated crucible,

children.text: sūtaḥ puṭito mriyate dhmātaḥ khoṭaṃ bhavatyeva ||
children.translated_text: the mercury, roasted in a puṭa, is killed; when blown, it indeed becomes a pellet.
Thus, with orpiment and realgar, and with pyrites and rasaka, together with darada and śikhi,

children.text: mriyate puṭasaṃyogād dhmātaṃ khoṭaṃ kṛtaṃ vimalam ||
children.translated_text: it is killed by the application of a puṭa; when blown, it is made into a stainless pellet.
From the combination of slag and pura, when they are blown, sattva falls from the slag,

children.text: nipatati satvaṃ rasasākaṃ janayati tadbhasma tasyāpi ||
children.translated_text: and the sattva, together with mercury, produces its ash as well.
Tin, rasa, sulfur, and orpiment, through conjunction with chalk, make an excellent parpaṭikā.
It colors sattva and orpiment, and mercury even without smoke.

children.text: evaṃ khoṭaṃ bījaṃ kṛtvā rañjanavidhinā surañjanaṃ kāryam
children.translated_text: Thus, after making the pellet into a seed, excellent coloring should be done by the coloring procedure.

children.text: triguṇaṃ rasasya hema saṃyojyaṃ tasya varabījam ||
children.translated_text: Gold, three times the mercury's quantity, should be joined to it; that is the best seed.
Now I shall explain, from mica-sattva, the stainless liquefaction that is the support of the whole mass of virtues.

children.text: sā hi nibadhnāti rasaṃ saṃmilitā milati ca sukhena ||
children.translated_text: For when it is combined, it binds mercury and mixes with it easily.
Mica, ground with the juice of <s>vajravallī</s> and mixed with sauvarcala salt,
when well cooked by niculapuṭas, becomes non-adherent and rasa-like in form.
By merely casting in powder of kapitinduka, drenched a hundred times with goat-water,
the mica-sattva, once liquefied, becomes like mercury in the crucible.
With an added casting made from powder arising from kañcukī bulb drenched a hundred times in its own juice,
mica-sattva remains melted; in the same way, all metals do so.
Mica, rubbed with hair oil and smeared with cow dung, in a diamond-hard crucible,
when very well blown, here its sattva soon floats like water.

children.text: gaganadrutiriha satve jñeyo hi rasasya sampradāyo 'yam
children.translated_text: In this tradition of mercury, the liquefaction of mica is to be understood as occurring here in the sattva.

children.text: prathamaṃ nipātya satvaṃ deyo vāpo drute tasmin ||
children.translated_text: First, after causing the sattva to fall, a casting should be given into that when it is molten.
Powder from the body of <s>suragopa</s> should be added with equal parts of <s>suradālī</s> fruits.
When the casting is given into molten gold, it remains melted, resembling that rasa.
Then, merely by casting powder of <s>suradālī</s> thoroughly treated with its own juice,

children.text: drutamevāste kanakaṃ labhate bhūyo na kaṭhinatvam ||
children.translated_text: the gold remains melted and does not again acquire hardness.
Ash of <s>suradālī</s>, melted, then dried with cow-water twenty-one times,
by casting makes the sharp metal placed in the crucible like water.
A bronze preparation cast with tortoise bone, bitumen, sheep bone, deer bone, and cow bone

children.text: jalasadṛśī bhavati sadā vāpo deyo drutāyāṃ tu ||
children.translated_text: always becomes like water; the casting should be given when it is molten.
A liquefaction not different from mica, non-adherent, joined in brief,
binds āroṭa and the king of rasas by means of a paired combination.
These liquefactions, with black aloe, musk, sugar, garlic, white rāmaṭha,
when warm, unite with mercury, after being rubbed with the juices of menstrual blood, palāśa, and seeds.
Thus the king of rasas, bound and used daily in a measure of one guñjā,
with just one pala produces a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
Now, according to the previously stated sequence of morsels, mercury digests in the prescribed manner;
these former liquefactions become productive of the fruit of the king of rasas.

children.text: samajīrṇaḥ śatavedhī dviguṇena rasaḥ sahasravedhī ca
children.translated_text: When equally digested, mercury pierces a hundredfold; with twice as much, it pierces a thousandfold,
and gradually it pierces ten millionfold through the addition of liquefaction in doubled and redoubled measure.
When sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four morsels have been digested,
then <s>rasendra</s> pierces metal merely at the sight of its smoke.
Thus even though <s>rasendra</s> is reddened and has digested the seed, if it lacks sāraṇā,

children.text: vyāpī na bhavati dehe loheṣvapyathavāpi hi ṣaṇḍhatāṃ yāti ||
children.translated_text: it does not become pervasive in the body; or even in metals it becomes impotent.
Of frogs, fish, turtles, sheep, leeches, snakes, boars, and the like,
one should combine the fat of any one of them and then cook the sāraṇā oil.
From the oil of <s>jyotiṣmatī</s>, <s>vibhītaka</s>, <s>karañja</s>, or bitter gourd, one at a time,
one should cook it with twice as much red decoction and four times as much milk.
With pomegranate, palāśa, bandhuka flowers, turmeric, and red-colored substances,
together with madder, lac juice, and sandalwood, this is the red group.
Coral, earth-worm impurity, and the excrement of bees, crows, and locusts,
and the ear-wax of buffalo cows, in order, form the paste, in a sixteenth part.
After taking mercury strained through cloth, in a full-length long crucible,

children.text: tadanu khalu taptataile pradrāvya samaṃ kṣiped bījam ||
children.translated_text: then, having melted it in hot oil, one should throw in an equal amount of seed.
One should cover the mouth of the crucible with a broad band threaded through two creepers,
with a cloth moistened with oil; then one should throw in the seed at the same time.
Mercury, applied by the sāraṇā method with seeds corresponding to the flesh,

children.text: akṣīyamāṇo milati ca bījair baddho bhavatyeva ||
children.translated_text: unites with the seeds without diminishing and, being bound, certainly becomes so.
In the same way, in a deep crucible, the king of rasas itself, moistened with sāraṇā oil,
after adding gold twice the quantity of mercury, should then be made to undergo sāraṇā.
With seed three times as much, one should make the mercury follow along while it is placed in the open.
A little lead should be added in the threefold sāraṇā.

children.text: kṛtvā mūṣāṃ dīrghāṃ bandhitatribhāgapraṇālikāṃ tāṃ ca
children.translated_text: Having made a long crucible, and that with a tube tied to one third of it,
at its front there should be an open crucible, perforated and coated with firm clay.
After placing mercury in that, furnished with sāraṇā oil, when it is heated,
having melted it, when an equal amount of gold is thrown in, the king of rasas unites.
Having made a long tube, six aṅgulas long, resembling a dhūrtaka flower,

children.text: mūṣāpyadho vilagnā kartavyā vai mṛdā lepyā ||
children.translated_text: a crucible too should be attached below, and it must be coated with clay.

children.text: aparā sūkṣmā nalikā kāryā saptāṃgulā sudṛḍhā
children.translated_text: Another fine tube should be made, seven aṅgulas long and very firm,

children.text: madhye praviśati ca yathā tadvatkāryā ca dṛḍhamukhā ||
children.translated_text: so that it enters in the middle; and likewise it should have a firm mouth.
Mercury is placed in that, furnished with sāraṇā oil, with its mouth stopped by madana.
Then, by means of the largest gold furnace, one should melt the gold.
Having placed it in the middle of that, one should turn the tip of the tube downward.

children.text: antarūrdhvaṃ bhārākrāntāṃ sarati raso nātra saṃdehaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pressed by a weight from within and above, the mercury flows; there is no doubt here.
Having made a crucible eight aṅgulas long, like a dhūrtaka flower, firm and smooth,

children.text: aparā madhyagatāpi ca sacchidrā ca saptāṃgulā kāryā ||
children.translated_text: another one, placed in the middle and perforated, should be made seven aṅgulas long.

children.text: niruddhatāṃ ca kṛtvā sūtaṃ prakṣipya tailasaṃyuktam
children.translated_text: After sealing it and placing mercury mixed with oil inside,

children.text: nirdhūmaṃ karṣāgnau sthāpya mūṣāṃ susaṃdhitāṃ kṛtvā ||
children.translated_text: having well joined the crucible, one should set it over a smokeless karṣa-fire.
A tube measuring a span should also be made on a firm crucible in front of it.

children.text: uttānaikā kāryā niśchidrā chidramudritā ca tanau ||
children.translated_text: One should make one upward-facing, without holes, and sealed at the opening on the body.

children.text: dattvā sūtaṃ pūrvaṃ sāraṇatailānvitaṃ nidhāpya bhuvi
children.translated_text: Having first put in mercury furnished with sāraṇā oil and set it on the ground,
in the upward-facing crucible, one should cover the seed in that.

children.text: svacchaṃ jñātvā ca tatastadbījaṃ chidrasaṃsthitaṃ kuryāt
children.translated_text: After recognizing it as clear, then one should set that seed in the hole.
The seed falls upon the mercury and binds it, without doubt.
And that open crucible should be made inverted, inserted by half an aṅgula.

children.text: nalikā kāryā vidhinā ūrdhve sūtastvadho bījam ||
children.translated_text: A tube should be made according to rule, with the mercury above and the seed below.

children.text: mūṣāṃ nirudhya vidhinā dhmātā koṣṭhe drutaṃ bījam
children.translated_text: Having sealed the crucible according to rule, when it is blown in the furnace, the seed is molten.

children.text: jñātvā parivartya tato nibadhnāti sūtarājaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: After recognizing this and then turning it over, it binds the king of mercury.
Or else, mercury applied by the sāraṇā method in a ḍamaruka apparatus,
<s>rasendra</s> flows according to rule, once one understands the skill of that operation.
Then one should digest that sārita <s>rasendra</s> by the procedure of morsels.
Again, mercury that has been made to flow pierces copper even by a hundred-millionth part.
Through the operation consisting of krāmaṇa and the like, mercury indeed flows according to rule,
because of its mobility and extreme lightness; therefore the seed should be made as a fine spray.

children.text: sarati sukhena ca sūto dahati mukhaṃ naiva hastapādādi
children.translated_text: And mercury flows easily; it does not burn the mouth, hands, feet, and the rest.
The rasa advances through conjunction with phaṇi, with pyrites, gold, and red ochre.
Through conjunction with pyrite-sattva and through conjunction with phaṇi, it melts quickly like lead,

children.text: dravati ca kanake sūtaḥ saṃsāryate vidhinā ||
children.translated_text: and mercury melts in gold; it is made to circulate according to rule.

children.text: tasmād dravyavidhāyī sūto bījena sārito laghunā
children.translated_text: Therefore mercury, producing substance, made to flow with a light seed,
equally made to flow and well bound, becomes fully turned in the crucible.
Mercury that has been made to flow and turned, when it unites with an equal seed, is called sārya,
when made to flow further with twice as much it is pratisārya, and when with three times as much it is anusārya.
The sārya pierces a hundredfold; when pratisārita it becomes a thousandfold piercer,
and when anusārita it pierces ten thousandfold, according to rule, after knowing its strength and weakness.

children.text: anusāritena tu samaḥ svacchaḥ sūtaḥ sāritastadanu
children.translated_text: Then clear mercury, equal to that which has been anusārita, is made sārita;

children.text: sa bhavati lakṣavedhī pratisāritaḥ prayutavedhī ca ||
children.translated_text: it becomes a hundred-thousandfold piercer, and when pratisārita a millionfold piercer.
Mercury, when anusārita, pierces a crore; it flows with the seed.
When pratisārita and anusārita, the mercury pierces ten crores.
When pratisārita it pierces an abja number, and when anusārita a kharva number,
thus by the sāraṇa operation it produces vedha as desired, according to rule.
Made sārita with what has been anusārita, it pierces copper counted by nikharvas.
But when pratisārita it pierces a padma number, and when well anusārita a śaṅkha number.
It should pierce twice the amount of substance; having added lead, one should cause it to carry on slowly,
until it brings forth all of the divine gold.
Thus ends the sixteenth instruction, consisting of sāraṇa, in the <s>Rasahṛdayatantra</s> composed by the glorious <s>Govindabhagavatpāda</s>, teacher of supreme-haṃsa renunciants.
Although the sāraṇa procedure has thus been performed, even the powerful king mercury, because of the operation,

children.text: saṃveṣṭya tiṣṭhati lohaṃ no viśati krāmaṇārahitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: remains enveloping the metal and does not enter it when it lacks krāmaṇa.

children.text: annaṃ vā dravyaṃ vā yathānupānena dhātuṣu kramate
